# Subaru Crosstrek, Forester, Impreza, Outback 8 Bolt Valve Cover Tightening Sequence

When working on the engine bay of a Subaru Crosstrek, Forester, Impreza, or Outback, replacing the valve cover is a common maintenance procedure. The specific challenge arises when you encounter the standard 8-bolt pattern used on these boxer engines. Unlike the four-bolt designs found on many V6 or inline-six architectures, an eight-bolt configuration introduces significant variables regarding stress distribution and gasket integrity. If the bolts are not torqued correctly, you risk warping the aluminum cover against the cylinder head, leading to immediate oil leaks or catastrophic failure under boost pressure.

The fundamental rule for any multi-bolt sealing surface is to follow a star pattern that moves from the center outward in concentric circles. For an 8-bolt arrangement, this means dividing the bolts into two alternating sets: Set A (bolts 1, 3, 5, 7) and Set B (bolts 2, 4, 6, 8). You must never torque all of Set A to full specification before touching a single bolt in Set B. This approach ensures that the gasket is compressed evenly across the entire surface area without creating "dishing" or high spots where oil could seep through the sealant or the gasket material itself.

The tightening process typically follows a multi-stage torque sequence, often referred to as "staged tightening." The manufacturer usually specifies three distinct stages for these Subaru engines:
1.  **Stage 1:** Tighten all bolts in both alternating sets (A and B) to approximately 30-40% of the final target torque.
2.  **Stage 2:** Increase the torque on all bolts to roughly 70-80% of the final specification.
3.  **Stage 3:** Perform a final pass to bring every bolt to the full specified torque value, strictly adhering to the star pattern established in Stage 1 and 2.

For these specific Subaru models, the final torque specification is generally between 7â9 ft-lbs (approx. 10â12 Nm), though you must always verify the exact number against the service manual for your specific engine displacement (2.0L vs 2.5L). Using a digital torque wrench or an angle-only tool is recommended to avoid over-torquing, which is a common mistake made when using impact guns that lack precise torque control. Over-torquing aluminum bolts can stretch them beyond their elastic limit, causing the bolt head to strip or the cover to crack internally.

There are also critical trade-offs regarding gasket materials. These engines often utilize a rubber or cork-rubber hybrid gasket. If you attempt to reuse an old gasket during a repair, you will almost certainly experience leaks because the sealing compound has likely hardened or degraded. Always install a fresh gasket and apply a thin layer of RTV sealant only if specified by the manufacturer, typically at the rear edge near the firewall to prevent coolant or oil intrusion into the spark plug wells.

A frequent pitfall involves neglecting the condition of the valve cover studs or bolts prior to installation. If the bolts are stretched from a previous removal, they may not achieve the correct clamping force even when torqued to spec. In high-stress scenarios like track days or heavy towing, compromised fasteners can lead to gasket blowouts. If in doubt about bolt integrity, replace them with new OEM-grade fasteners rather than reusing hardware that has seen prior service cycles.

Finally, remember to disconnect the battery before working on ignition coils or spark plug wires while the valve cover is removed. This prevents accidental shorts and ensures safety during the installation process. Once the cover is seated and torqued in stages, perform a visual inspection of the gasket edges to ensure no debris was trapped underneath before tightening fully.
